title: Scientists tame a single antimatter particle for months, opening route to fundamental physics test
excerpt: A single positron has been cooled close to absolute zero, isolated from ordinary matter and placed under quantum control. The achievement gives physicists a new tool for testing whether matter and antimatter really obey the same fundamental laws.
content:
Antimatter tends to belong either to the most fundamental reaches of physics or the most speculative corners of science fiction. A new experiment has brought it into a much more controlled setting: one particle, held almost motionless and kept under observation for months.

Physicists at Northwestern University have trapped a single positron, the antimatter counterpart of the electron, and coaxed it into a highly controlled quantum state. The researchers say this is the first time such control has been achieved with an individual positron.

The result is what the scientists call a “one-positron quantum cyclotron”. Described in the peer-reviewed journal Physical Review Letters, the experiment potentially clears the way for an exceptionally demanding comparison between matter and antimatter. The research paper was published on 21 October 2026.  If future measurements reveal a difference where established theory says there should be none, the consequences could be profound.

A positron has the same mass as an electron but carries the opposite electric charge. The difficulty with studying one is that antimatter cannot simply be put into an ordinary physical container. When a positron meets an electron, the matter and antimatter particles annihilate. Consequently, an experimental system designed to hold a positron needs what amounts to a container without conventional walls.

The Northwestern University team achieved this using a Penning trap, in which electric and magnetic fields confine the particle without requiring it to rest against material surfaces. The journal paper reports that the positron can be suspended indefinitely in the trap’s magnetic field.

As explained in Northwestern University’s account of the research, the positrons used in the experiment originated from the radioactive decay of sodium-22. The resulting fast-moving particle first had to be dramatically slowed before being guided into the near-perfect vacuum of the trap.  The apparatus itself was cooled to around 300 millikelvins, equivalent to 0.3 degrees above absolute zero. Under these conditions, the researchers brought the positron into its quantum ground state. The trapped positron has remained safely confined for months. This extreme cooling matters because thermal motion can interfere with the exceptionally delicate measurements the researchers want to make.

Turning one positron into a quantum instrument

Simply keeping the particle alive, however, is only part of the achievement. The researchers demonstrated that they could manipulate and detect the positron’s individual quantum energy states. Using precisely tuned microwaves, energy can be supplied to the particle in tiny amounts and the resulting transitions between quantum states detected.

In effect, the trapped particle becomes a highly controllable microscopic experimental system: an artificial atom-like structure whose quantum behaviour can be interrogated with extraordinary sensitivity. This degree of control is important because the experiment is intended to lead to an ultra-precise measurement of the positron’s magnetic moment, a fundamental property describing how the particle interacts with a magnetic field.

The importance lies not only in measuring the positron itself, but in comparing that result with the corresponding property of the electron. The new study states that measurements using positron and electron quantum cyclotrons should provide the most stringent test in the lepton sector of CPT invariance, a fundamental symmetry underlying modern particle physics.

Putting the Standard Model under pressure

The Standard Model experiment matters because modern particle physics has an unusual problem. The Standard Model has repeatedly produced extremely accurate predictions, yet physicists know that it does not provide a complete description of nature. Among the questions it does not resolve is why the observable universe contains overwhelmingly more matter than antimatter.  That imbalance presents an enduring puzzle. The early universe might be expected to have produced matter and antimatter together, yet the visible universe today is dominated by matter. The Northwestern experiment approaches this enormous cosmological question by studying one of nature’s simplest possible systems.

Gerald Gabrielse, who led the study, puts the objective directly: “We know the Standard Model has to be wrong somewhere — or at least incomplete.” He adds that the strategy is to examine “the most fundamental and simple systems” with great precision in the hope of identifying where the theory breaks down. Gabrielse is Board of Trustees Professor in Physics at Northwestern University and director of its Center for Fundamental Physics at Low Energy. His research group specialises in highly precise tests of the Standard Model and searches for physics beyond it.

Precision as a route to discovery

Rather than trying to discover an entirely new particle by smashing particles together at ever higher energies, this type of research takes another route: making extraordinarily precise measurements of particles already known to science. There is good precedent. The researchers’ earlier work produced an electron magnetic-moment measurement with a precision of about one part in 10 trillion. The ambition is now to bring corresponding quantum measurement techniques to the positron and compare the results.

The achievement reported this month is therefore not the final matter-versus-antimatter result. It establishes the experimental platform through which a substantially more precise comparison can be pursued.

According to the Physical Review Letters paper, trapping the individual positron in a quantum cyclotron opens the possibility of determining its magnetic moment at substantially higher precision than was possible using classical cyclotron motion.  Under current theory, the coming electron and positron measurements should agree as required by the relevant fundamental symmetry. A confirmed discrepancy would therefore demand an explanation beyond the present Standard Model.

Gabrielse sets the stakes high: “Current theories suggest that there will be no difference in the two measurements. If it turns out they are not equal, that would be the biggest discovery in physics in the last century.”
